newsitem.title: USA: Mexico gains by retiring costly debt - US investors.
newsitem.headline: Mexico gains by retiring costly debt - US investors.

text.p: U.S. investors applauded Mexico's effort Tuesday to use fresh debt to prepay some of its more costly obligations that were backed by the country's oil revenues.
On Tuesday, Mexico announced a massive debt restructing plan to buy up $6.0 billion in floating rate notes due 2001 with proceeds from recent debt offerings.
"I view it as a sign that they are more efficient at liability management," said one U.S. speculative investor. "It's a way of eliminating expensive debt."

Mexico had issued the $6.0 billion of oil revenue collateralized notes in August 1996, when the country was just emerging from recession and reintegrating itself into the international capital markets.
The issue appealed to international investors because it received investment grade credit ratings based on the firm support of Mexican oil revenues.
Conditions in the emering markets have improved markedly over the past year, however, and Mexico no longer needed the firm backing of its oil proceeds.

"It's a nice sign of relative strength that they are retiring one of the first things they issued when they were in trouble," said another U.S. investor. "The world's awash in liquidity, so why not refund this stuff."
Given its oil flows, the Mexican government could always reissue oil revenue collateralized paper, and it can float the paper at more favorable prices, investors said.
"It was a smart way of not paying (in 2001) a facility that was expensive," the investor said. "Mexico always has the oil receivables and they can always put the structure back."
To buy back the paper, Mexico will rely on various funding mechanisms, among which will be an issue of $1.0 billion five-year floating rate notes.
In addition, Mexico will raise the amount of a 10-year note issued in January 1997 to $1.5 billion from $1.0 billion.
Market sources said that the expansion of the offer relieved price pressure that had developed when a major Mexican investor bought up a large share of the issue.
"There was talk that some big speculator went in and bought up the whole (2007) issue and a lot of guys were feeling pain about it," said one Brady bond trader.
The Brady bond market reacted favorably to the news. In afternoon trade, Mexican Discounts MXFLL19=RR gained 1/2 tp 93-1/2, while the country's global bonds due 2026 MXUMS=RR rose 1/4 to 114-1/2 bid.
